[Block B] Prototype the core: a training pipeline + a served model + basic monitoring. [Block C] Present it as a design doc + working prototype — exactly the artifact senior ML interviews want.

units.title: Thinking at system scale
units.text: Problem framing, distributed training, scaled data pipelines, cost/latency and case studies build ML system-design judgment. Re-read your design doc critically.
units.mastery: Walk an interviewer through your ML system design: objective, data, baseline, serving, monitoring, and the top three tradeoffs.

units.text:
Pick a real, meaningful ML problem; define the objective and metric and assemble/clean the data.
🎥 Watch: Revisit Chip Huyen's framing + your EDA notes.
💻 Code: Write the capstone problem statement and success metric, and load/clean the data.

units.title: Feature & label pipelines
units.text:
Build leak-free feature and label pipelines with point-in-time correctness.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your feature-engineering + feature-store work.
💻 Code: Build the feature/label pipeline with tests and no future leakage.

units.title: Modeling & evaluation
units.text:
Baseline -> improved model with honest cross-validation, the right metric, and error analysis.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your evaluation toolkit.
💻 Code: Train baseline + improved models, evaluate rigorously, and do error analysis.

units.title: Serving
units.text:
Serve the model as an API with schemas, containerized, ready for monitoring.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your serving + MLOps work.
💻 Code: Serve the model (FastAPI/BentoML), containerized, with a typed API.

units.title: Monitoring & writeup
units.text:
Add drift/performance monitoring and write the portfolio narrative + model card.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your monitoring + interpretability work.
💻 Code: Add monitoring, write the README/model card, and record a demo.

units.title: ML-product capstone — build & ship
units.text: [Block A] Assemble the full ML product: data -> features -> model -> API, reproducible and tracked (MLflow/DVC). [Block B] Add monitoring (drift, performance), interpretability (SHAP) and CI/CD. [Block C] Ship it: repo, model card, demo — your flagship Data Science / ML portfolio project.

units.title: Perceptron & MLPs
units.text:
A neuron is a weighted sum + a nonlinearity; stack them into layers (an MLP) and you can approximate any function (universal approximation).
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — Neural Networks ch.1; Andrej Karpathy — 'The spelled-out intro to neural networks' (micrograd).
💻 Code: Implement a single neuron and a 2-layer MLP forward pass in NumPy.

units.title: Backpropagation from scratch
units.text:
Backprop is reverse-mode autodiff: compute local gradients over a computation graph and chain them back to update weights.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — micrograd ('building an autograd engine'); 3Blue1Brown — backpropagation.
💻 Code: Build a tiny autograd engine (micrograd-style) and train an MLP on a toy dataset.

units.title: Activations & initialization
units.text:
ReLU/GELU/sigmoid/tanh and why they matter (vanishing gradients); why init (Xavier/He) makes training even possible.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — makemore (activations, init, batchnorm); search 'weight initialization deep learning'.
💻 Code: Compare training with different activations + inits and watch gradients vanish or explode.

units.title: Loss functions & optimizers (Adam)
units.text:
Cross-entropy vs MSE, and the optimizers (SGD, momentum, RMSProp, Adam) that shape convergence.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Adam optimizer explained'; Karpathy — makemore.
💻 Code: Train the same net with SGD vs Adam and compare convergence.

units.title: Regularization: dropout & batchnorm
units.text:
Dropout, batch/layer norm, weight decay and early stopping — the tricks that make deep nets generalize and train stably.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — makemore (batchnorm); search 'dropout batchnorm explained'.
💻 Code: Add dropout + batchnorm to your net and measure the effect on overfitting.

units.title: Neural net from scratch (NumPy) then PyTorch
units.text: [Block A] Build a full MLP from scratch in NumPy: forward, backprop, an optimizer, a training loop — train it on MNIST-ish data. [Block B] Reimplement it in PyTorch and match the results; note what the framework automates (autograd, optimizers). [Block C] Write up 'what a neural net really computes' with your from-scratch code — it proves deep understanding.

units.title: What a network really computes
units.text: Neurons/MLPs, backprop, activations/init, losses/optimizers and regularization are the machinery of every deep model. Re-run your micrograd and watch the gradients flow.
units.mastery: Explain backprop as reverse-mode autodiff, and why initialization and normalization matter for training.

units.title: PyTorch: tensors & autograd
units.text:
Tensors (GPU arrays), autograd (the dynamic computation graph), and requires_grad / backward().
🎥 Watch: PyTorch official 'Learn the Basics' tutorial.
💻 Code: Recreate your from-scratch net using torch tensors + autograd; verify gradients with .backward().

units.title: nn.Module & training loops
units.text:
Defining models with nn.Module, the canonical training loop (forward -> loss -> backward -> step), and datasets/dataloaders.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch tutorials; fast.ai — Practical Deep Learning lesson 1.
💻 Code: Write a clean, reusable training loop with nn.Module, an optimizer and a DataLoader.

units.title: Data loading & augmentation
units.text:
Dataset/DataLoader, batching, and augmentation to fight overfitting and expand data.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — data loading tutorial; search 'data augmentation'.
💻 Code: Build a Dataset + DataLoader with augmentation and visualize the augmented batches.

units.title: Training tricks: schedules, mixed precision
units.text:
LR schedules (warmup, cosine), mixed precision (amp) for speed/memory, gradient clipping and checkpointing.
🎥 Watch: Search 'PyTorch mixed precision amp' and 'learning rate schedule warmup cosine'.
💻 Code: Add a cosine LR schedule + mixed precision to your training loop and measure the speedup.

units.title: Debugging deep nets
units.text:
Diagnosing training: loss not dropping, overfitting, NaNs — and Karpathy's recipe for training neural nets.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'A Recipe for Training Neural Networks' (blog); search 'debugging neural networks'.
💻 Code: Deliberately break a training run (bad LR, no shuffle) and diagnose each issue from the loss curves.

units.title: Image classifier end-to-end in PyTorch
units.text: [Block A] Build a CNN image classifier in PyTorch on a real dataset (CIFAR-10 or your own): Dataset, model, training loop. [Block B] Add augmentation, an LR schedule, mixed precision and checkpointing; track with TensorBoard/W&B. [Block C] Push past a strong accuracy target and write up the training choices — a solid deep-learning portfolio piece.

units.title: Training that converges
units.text: Tensors/autograd, nn.Module loops, data loading, training tricks and debugging are the day-to-day of deep learning. Re-read Karpathy's recipe.
units.mastery: Walk through one full training step in PyTorch, and your checklist when the loss won't drop.

units.title: Convolutions & CNN architectures
units.text:
Convolutions (local, shared weights), pooling, and how CNNs build hierarchical features — the conv/pool/FC pattern.
🎥 Watch: Stanford CS231n — CNNs; StatQuest — convolutional neural networks.
💻 Code: Implement a conv layer forward pass by hand, then build a small CNN in PyTorch.

units.title: Classic architectures (ResNet, etc.)
units.text:
LeNet -> AlexNet -> VGG -> ResNet (skip connections that enable very deep nets); what each innovation solved.
🎥 Watch: Search 'ResNet explained'; CS231n architectures lecture.
💻 Code: Build a small ResNet with skip connections and train it; compare to a plain deep CNN.

units.title: Transfer learning
units.text:
Reusing pretrained backbones (ImageNet) and fine-tuning — strong results with little data.
🎥 Watch: fast.ai — transfer learning; the PyTorch transfer-learning tutorial.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a small custom dataset and beat training-from-scratch.

units.title: Detection & segmentation intro
units.text:
Beyond classification: object detection (YOLO/Faster R-CNN) and segmentation (U-Net/Mask R-CNN) at a high level.
🎥 Watch: Search 'object detection YOLO explained' and 'image segmentation U-Net'.
💻 Code: Run a pretrained detector (YOLO) on your images and interpret the boxes/scores.

units.title: Vision in practice
units.text:
Data quality, class imbalance, evaluation (mAP/IoU), and deploying a vision model.
🎥 Watch: Search 'computer vision production pitfalls'.
💻 Code: Evaluate your fine-tuned model with a confusion matrix + per-class metrics and find its failure modes.

units.title: Fine-tune a CNN for a real vision task
units.text: [Block A] Pick a real vision task/dataset; set up data, augmentation and a pretrained backbone. [Block B] Fine-tune it, tune the head/LR, and evaluate rigorously (per-class, failure cases). [Block C] Serve it behind a small API with a demo UI and write up the transfer-learning approach — a portfolio CV project.

units.title: Seeing with networks
units.text: Convolutions, classic architectures, transfer learning, detection/segmentation and practical evaluation are the CV toolkit. Re-read your model's failure modes.
units.mastery: Why do skip connections let nets go deeper, and when does transfer learning beat training from scratch?

units.title: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs
units.text:
Modeling sequences with recurrence, the vanishing-gradient problem, and how LSTM/GRU gates fix long-range memory.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'The Unreasonable Effectiveness of RNNs' (blog); StatQuest — RNNs/LSTMs.
💻 Code: Build a character-level RNN/LSTM in PyTorch and generate text.

units.title: Word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe)
units.text:
Dense word vectors capturing meaning (king - man + woman = queen); skip-gram/CBOW and how embeddings are learned.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated Word2vec'.
💻 Code: Train word2vec on a corpus and explore analogies + nearest neighbors.

units.title: Tokenization & text preprocessing
units.text:
From text to tokens: word/subword (BPE) tokenization, normalization, and why tokenization shapes everything downstream.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build the GPT Tokenizer'; HuggingFace — tokenizers.
💻 Code: Compare word-level vs BPE tokenization on a corpus; inspect the vocab and OOV behavior.

units.title: seq2seq & attention
units.text:
Encoder-decoder for translation/summarization, and attention as the fix for the fixed-context bottleneck — the bridge to Transformers.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'Visualizing seq2seq with attention'; Stanford CS224N — attention.
💻 Code: Build a small seq2seq model with attention for a toy translation/copy task.

units.title: Classic NLP tasks
units.text:
Text classification, NER, sentiment and NLP evaluation — the tasks LLMs now subsume but you should understand.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace NLP course (early chapters); CS224N.
💻 Code: Build a text classifier (embeddings + a small net) and evaluate it properly.

units.title: Text classifier / seq2seq model
units.text: [Block A] Build a solid text model: a classifier (embeddings -> net) or a seq2seq-with-attention for a small task. [Block B] Add proper tokenization, training, and NLP-appropriate evaluation. [Block C] Write up how attention solved the seq2seq bottleneck — the perfect setup for next week's Transformers.

units.title: Modeling sequences
units.text: RNNs/LSTMs, embeddings, tokenization, seq2seq + attention and classic NLP are the pre-Transformer world — and attention is the thread into it. Re-read the Illustrated Word2vec.
units.mastery: Why do RNNs struggle with long sequences, and what problem does attention solve in seq2seq?

units.title: The attention mechanism, deep
units.text:
Query/key/value attention: every token attends to every other, weighted by relevance — the core operation of modern AI.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — attention; Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated Transformer'.
💻 Code: Implement scaled dot-product attention from scratch in PyTorch and verify shapes/softmax.

units.title: The Transformer: encoder / decoder
units.text:
The full architecture: multi-head attention, feed-forward blocks, residual connections + layernorm, encoder vs decoder stacks.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — Illustrated Transformer; skim 'Attention Is All You Need'.
💻 Code: Assemble a single Transformer block (attention + FFN + residual + norm) in PyTorch.

units.title: Self-attention, multi-head, positional encoding
units.text:
Multiple heads capture different relations; positional encodings inject order into an otherwise order-blind mechanism.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build GPT' (self-attention section).
💻 Code: Add multi-head attention + positional encodings to your block and visualize an attention matrix.

units.title: BERT vs GPT families
units.text:
Encoder-only (BERT, bidirectional, understanding) vs decoder-only (GPT, autoregressive, generation) vs encoder-decoder (T5) — and what each is for.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated GPT-2' and 'Illustrated BERT'.
💻 Code: Load BERT and GPT-2 from HuggingFace and compare what each does on the same text.

units.title: Building a transformer block
units.text:
Putting it together into a working decoder-only LM: embeddings, N blocks, a head, and the training objective.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build GPT: from scratch'.
💻 Code: Wire embeddings + stacked blocks + an output head into a tiny GPT and do a forward pass.

units.title: Transformer from scratch (nanoGPT-style)
units.text: [Block A] Build a decoder-only Transformer (GPT) from scratch in PyTorch following Karpathy's 'Let's build GPT': attention, blocks, positional encodings. [Block B] Train it on a text corpus (tiny-shakespeare or your own) and generate samples. [Block C] Annotate every component with what it does + why; publish a 'built a GPT from scratch' repo — a flagship AI project.
units.demo: GPT / Transformer implemented from scratch in PyTorch (nanoGPT-style).

units.title: Attention is the engine
units.text: Attention, the full Transformer, multi-head + positions, the BERT/GPT split and a working block are the foundation of everything modern in AI. Re-watch Karpathy's GPT build.
units.mastery: Explain self-attention with Q/K/V in one paragraph, and why positional encodings are necessary.

units.title: Pretraining objectives (MLM, CLM)
units.text:
Masked language modeling (BERT) vs causal/next-token (GPT); how self-supervised pretraining learns from raw text at scale.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — Illustrated BERT; search 'MLM vs CLM pretraining'.
💻 Code: Implement next-token (causal) training for your nanoGPT and track the loss.

units.title: Tokenizers: BPE & SentencePiece
units.text:
Byte-pair encoding and SentencePiece: how subword vocabularies are built, and their effect on cost and multilinguality.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build the GPT Tokenizer'; HuggingFace tokenizers.
💻 Code: Train a BPE tokenizer on your corpus and plug it into your GPT.

units.title: Scaling laws & model families
units.text:
How loss scales with params/data/compute (Chinchilla), and the landscape of open vs closed model families.
🎥 Watch: Search 'scaling laws Chinchilla explained'.
💻 Code: Train your small GPT at 2-3 sizes and plot loss vs params/compute — see scaling firsthand.

units.title: The HuggingFace ecosystem
units.text:
transformers, datasets, tokenizers and the Hub; loading, running and sharing pretrained models the standard way.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace — NLP course (using Transformers).
💻 Code: Load a pretrained model + tokenizer from the Hub, run inference, and push a model/dataset.

units.title: Fine-tuning basics
units.text:
Full fine-tuning a pretrained model on a downstream task, and the train/eval loop with the HuggingFace Trainer.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace — fine-tuning a pretrained model.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a small pretrained model (e.g. DistilBERT) on a classification task with Trainer.

units.title: Train a small GPT on a custom corpus
units.text: [Block A] Take your nanoGPT, add a trained BPE tokenizer and causal pretraining, and train on a corpus you care about. [Block B] Scale it up a little, add eval (perplexity) and sampling controls (temperature/top-k). [Block C] Write up the pretraining run + scaling observations — deep, credible AI portfolio content.

units.title: How LLMs are made
units.text: Pretraining objectives, tokenizers, scaling laws, the HuggingFace ecosystem and fine-tuning basics are how raw text becomes a language model. Re-read your loss/perplexity curves.
units.mastery: Contrast MLM and causal pretraining, and what scaling laws say about spending compute on params vs data.

units.title: Inference, sampling & decoding
units.text:
How an LLM generates: logits -> sampling (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p), and why decoding settings change outputs.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM sampling temperature top-p explained'.
💻 Code: Take a HuggingFace LLM and generate with different decoding settings; observe the effect.

units.title: Prompting techniques
units.text:
Zero/few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured prompts, and system/user roles — reliable behavior from a fixed model.
🎥 Watch: Search 'prompt engineering guide'; Anthropic prompt-engineering docs.
💻 Code: Take a task and improve results measurably by iterating prompts (zero-shot -> few-shot -> CoT).

units.title: Context, tokens & cost
units.text:
Context windows, tokenization cost, managing long inputs (truncation, chunking), and latency/price tradeoffs.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM context window tokens explained'.
💻 Code: Measure tokens + cost for prompts of different sizes and build a token budget for an app.

units.title: LLM APIs & the ecosystem
units.text:
Calling LLM APIs (messages, system prompts, streaming, tools), and the open-vs-hosted landscape.
🎥 Watch: Read a major provider's messages/API docs (e.g. Anthropic/OpenAI).
💻 Code: Build a small app that calls an LLM API with a system prompt and streams the response.

units.title: LLM evaluation
units.text:
Why eval is hard, and approaches: golden sets, rubric/LLM-as-judge, and task-specific metrics — eval-driven development.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — evaluating LLM apps; search 'LLM evaluation methods'.
💻 Code: Build a small eval harness (golden examples + an LLM-as-judge rubric) for a task.

units.title: LLM app with strong prompting + an eval harness
units.text: [Block A] Build a real LLM feature (summarizer, extractor, assistant) via an API with a solid system prompt. [Block B] Add structured output, error handling, streaming and a token/cost budget. [Block C] Build an eval harness (golden set + LLM-judge) and iterate prompts against it — eval-driven, portfolio-grade.

units.title: Using LLMs well
units.text: Decoding, prompting, context/cost, APIs and evaluation are the practical foundation of building with LLMs. Re-read your eval results.
units.mastery: How does temperature/top-p change generation, and why is a golden-set + judge eval better than eyeballing outputs?

units.title: Embeddings, deep
units.text:
Text embeddings map meaning to vectors; similarity search, and choosing/measuring an embedding model.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — illustrated embeddings; search 'text embeddings explained'.
💻 Code: Embed a corpus with an embedding model and build semantic search over it (cosine similarity).

units.title: Vector databases (pgvector, etc.)
units.text:
Storing + searching embeddings at scale: ANN indexes (HNSW) and pgvector/FAISS/other stores.
🎥 Watch: Search 'vector database explained'; pgvector docs.
💻 Code: Load embeddings into pgvector (or FAISS) and run fast approximate nearest-neighbor search.

units.title: RAG architecture
units.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant chunks, put them in the prompt, generate a grounded answer — the dominant enterprise LLM pattern.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG explained'; Chip Huyen / Anthropic on RAG.
💻 Code: Build a minimal RAG: chunk -> embed -> retrieve -> prompt -> answer over your own docs.

units.title: Chunking, retrieval & reranking
units.text:
Chunking strategies, hybrid search (keyword + vector), reranking and query rewriting — where RAG quality is won or lost.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG chunking strategies reranking'.
💻 Code: Improve your RAG's retrieval with better chunking + a reranker; measure the answer-quality lift.

units.title: RAG evaluation
units.text:
Evaluating RAG: retrieval metrics (recall/precision@k) + answer faithfulness/groundedness (RAGAS-style).
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG evaluation RAGAS'.
💻 Code: Build a RAG eval set and score retrieval + faithfulness; find and fix the weakest link.

units.title: Production RAG over your own corpus
units.text: [Block A] Build a real RAG system over a corpus you care about (your notes, docs, a codebase): ingest -> chunk -> embed -> vector store. [Block B] Add hybrid retrieval + reranking, query rewriting, citations, and a chat UI/API. [Block C] Add a RAG eval harness (retrieval + faithfulness) and iterate; ship it — a flagship AI portfolio project.
units.demo: Production RAG over a real corpus: hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, eval harness.

units.title: Grounding LLMs in data
units.text: Embeddings, vector DBs, the RAG loop, chunking/reranking and RAG eval are the most in-demand LLM skill set right now. Re-read your RAG eval scores.
units.mastery: Walk through a RAG query end to end, and name the two places retrieval quality most often breaks.

units.title: Full fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA
units.text:
When to fine-tune, full vs parameter-efficient (LoRA freezes the model and trains small adapters; QLoRA adds quantization).
🎥 Watch: Sebastian Raschka — LoRA/fine-tuning; search 'LoRA QLoRA explained'.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a small open model with LoRA (PEFT) on a task dataset.

units.title: PEFT & adapters
units.text:
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, adapters, prefix/prompt tuning) — big gains, tiny trainable footprints.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace PEFT docs; Sebastian Raschka.
💻 Code: Compare LoRA rank / target-module choices and their effect on quality + trainable params.

units.title: Instruction tuning; RLHF/DPO intuition
units.text:
Turning a base model into an assistant: instruction tuning, and preference alignment (RLHF, DPO) at an intuition level.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RLHF explained' and 'DPO direct preference optimization'.
💻 Code: Instruction-tune a small model on an instruction dataset and compare to the base model.

units.title: Quantization & distillation
units.text:
Shrinking models for cheaper inference: quantization (int8/int4, GGUF) and distillation (a small model learns from a big one).
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM quantization explained GGUF' and 'knowledge distillation'.
💻 Code: Quantize your fine-tuned model to int4 and measure the size/latency vs quality tradeoff.

units.title: When to tune vs RAG vs prompt
units.text:
The decision framework: prompting for behavior, RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for style/format/skill — and their costs.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen; search 'fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting'.
💻 Code: Take one task and solve it three ways (prompt, RAG, fine-tune); compare quality, cost and effort.

units.title: Fine-tune an open LLM with LoRA
units.text: [Block A] Pick a task where fine-tuning helps (style, format, a domain skill) and prepare a clean instruction dataset. [Block B] Fine-tune an open model with LoRA/QLoRA; evaluate against the base model + a prompted baseline. [Block C] Quantize + serve it, and write up the tune-vs-RAG-vs-prompt decision — a strong applied-AI portfolio piece.
units.demo: Fine-tuned an open LLM with LoRA/QLoRA and served it.

units.title: Adapting models to you
units.text: Full vs PEFT fine-tuning, instruction tuning/alignment, quantization/distillation and the tune-vs-RAG-vs-prompt decision are how you shape models. Re-read your three-way comparison.
units.mastery: How does LoRA fine-tune a model without touching most of its weights, and when do you fine-tune instead of RAG?

units.title: Agent concepts: ReAct & planning
units.text:
Agents = an LLM + tools + a loop; ReAct (reason + act), planning, and the reason-act-observe cycle.
🎥 Watch: Search 'ReAct agents explained'; Anthropic — 'Building effective agents'.
💻 Code: Build a minimal ReAct loop by hand (no framework): reason -> call a tool -> observe -> repeat.

units.title: Tool use & function calling
units.text:
Giving models tools via function/tool calling: schemas, the call loop, and parsing/validating tool outputs.
🎥 Watch: A provider's tool-use/function-calling docs (Anthropic/OpenAI).
💻 Code: Give your agent 2-3 real tools (search, calculator, an API) via function calling and let it use them.

units.title: Frameworks vs framework-light
units.text:
LangChain/LlamaIndex/LangGraph vs writing it yourself; why framework-light is often better for control and debugging.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic — 'Building effective agents' (the framework caution); search 'do you need langchain'.
💻 Code: Rebuild your agent both with a framework and framework-light; compare control and debuggability.

units.title: Memory & state
units.text:
Short-term (context) vs long-term memory (a vector store), conversation state and scratchpads.
🎥 Watch: Search 'agent memory patterns'.
💻 Code: Add long-term memory (a vector store the agent reads/writes) so it recalls past interactions.

units.title: Multi-agent systems
units.text:
When multiple specialized agents beat one (orchestrator/worker, debate, review), and the coordination cost.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic; search 'multi-agent systems LLM'.
💻 Code: Build a 2-agent setup (a worker + a reviewer/critic) and show it beats a single agent on a task.

units.title: Tool-using agent for a real task (fleet-style)
units.text: [Block A] Build an agent that does a genuinely useful task with tools (like your own bot fleet): define the tools + the loop, framework-light. [Block B] Add memory, error handling and guardrails; make it reliable, not a demo. [Block C] Deploy it (a scheduled job or a bot) and document the design — a flagship, on-brand AI portfolio project.
units.demo: Autonomous tool-using agent (framework-light) that completes a real task.

units.title: Agents that act
units.text: ReAct + planning, tool use, framework choices, memory and multi-agent patterns are how LLMs do things, not just talk. Re-read Anthropic's 'Building effective agents'.
units.mastery: Describe the reason-act-observe loop, and when a multi-agent design actually beats a single well-prompted agent.

units.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol), deep
units.text:
MCP standardizes how models connect to tools/data (servers expose tools/resources/prompts) — the 'USB-C for AI tools'.
🎥 Watch: modelcontextprotocol.io docs; search 'Model Context Protocol explained'.
💻 Code: Read the MCP spec and run an existing MCP server with a client.

units.title: Building MCP servers
units.text:
Writing an MCP server that exposes tools + resources so any MCP client (Claude, IDEs) can use your data/actions.
🎥 Watch: MCP docs — build a server (Python/TS SDK).
💻 Code: Build an MCP server exposing 2-3 tools over your data (e.g. your data platform) and connect a client.

units.title: Agent-orchestration patterns
units.text:
Orchestrator/worker, routing, chaining and evaluator-optimizer loops — deterministic control around non-deterministic models.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic — 'Building effective agents' (patterns).
💻 Code: Implement an orchestrator that routes a task to the right tool/sub-agent deterministically.

units.title: Evaluation & guardrails
units.text:
Evaluating agents (task success, trajectory), and guardrails: input/output validation, allow-lists and human-in-the-loop.
🎥 Watch: Search 'evaluating AI agents'; guardrails frameworks.
💻 Code: Add guardrails (a tool allow-list, output validation) + a task-success eval to your agent.

units.title: Cost, latency & reliability
units.text:
Agents are expensive and flaky by default: caching, step limits, retries, and cost/latency budgets.
🎥 Watch: Search 'production AI agents reliability cost'.
💻 Code: Add step limits, caching and retries; measure and cut your agent's cost per task.

units.title: MCP server + agent over your data platform
units.text: [Block A] Build an MCP server that exposes your Data-Engineering platform (query data, check pipeline status) as tools. [Block B] Build an agent that uses it to answer real questions / do real tasks, with orchestration + guardrails. [Block C] Add evaluation + cost controls and document it — this ties your DE, AI and infra work into one showcase.
units.demo: MCP server + agent exposing a data platform as LLM tools.

units.title: Wiring agents to tools
units.text: MCP, building servers, orchestration patterns, evaluation/guardrails and cost/reliability are how agents become dependable products. Re-read your guardrails.
units.mastery: What problem does MCP standardize, and what are the three things that keep a production agent reliable and affordable?

units.title: Serving LLMs (vLLM, TGI)
units.text:
Efficient LLM serving with vLLM/TGI: continuous batching, paged attention, and why naive serving is slow and expensive.
🎥 Watch: Search 'vLLM paged attention'; the vLLM docs.
💻 Code: Serve an open model with vLLM and benchmark throughput vs a naive HuggingFace pipeline.

units.title: Inference optimization: KV cache, batching
units.text:
The KV cache, continuous batching, quantization and speculative decoding — the levers of fast, cheap inference.
🎥 Watch: Search 'KV cache explained' and 'continuous batching LLM'.
💻 Code: Measure the effect of the KV cache + batching on latency/throughput for your served model.

units.title: Observability: tracing & evals
units.text:
Tracing LLM apps (spans, tokens, cost), online evals, and catching quality regressions in production.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM observability tracing' (LangSmith/Langfuse concepts).
💻 Code: Add tracing (tokens, latency, cost per request) + an online eval to an LLM app.

units.title: Guardrails & prompt-injection defense
units.text:
Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and defenses: input/output filtering, allow-lists, and untrusted-content isolation.
🎥 Watch: Search 'prompt injection explained'; the OWASP LLM Top 10.
💻 Code: Attack your own LLM app with prompt injection, then add defenses and re-test.

units.title: Cost at scale
units.text:
Token economics, caching, model routing (small model first) and batching — running AI affordably.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM cost optimization strategies'.
💻 Code: Add a cache + model-routing (cheap model first, escalate) to an app and measure the cost drop.

units.title: Deploy an LLM app with evals + guardrails
units.text: [Block A] Take your RAG/agent app and deploy it properly (vLLM or an API) with schemas + streaming. [Block B] Add observability (tracing, cost), online evals, and guardrails (injection defense, output validation). [Block C] Load-test it, add cost controls, and document the LLMOps setup — a portfolio production-AI piece.

units.title: Operating AI in production
units.text: Serving, inference optimization, observability, guardrails and cost control separate an AI demo from an AI product. Re-run your injection tests.
units.mastery: What does continuous batching + a KV cache do for LLM serving, and how do you defend against prompt injection?

units.title: Multimodal models
units.text:
Vision-language models (CLIP, LLaVA, GPT-4V-style): how images + text share an embedding space and enable new tasks.
🎥 Watch: Search 'CLIP explained' and 'multimodal LLMs'.
💻 Code: Use CLIP for zero-shot image classification / image-text search.

units.title: Diffusion models (generation)
units.text:
How diffusion generates images by iterative denoising; latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) and conditioning.
🎥 Watch: Search 'how diffusion models work'; Jay Alammar — illustrated stable diffusion.
💻 Code: Run Stable Diffusion, then read a from-scratch diffusion tutorial to understand the denoising loop.

units.title: Structured generation & function calling
units.text:
Constraining LLM output to schemas/JSON/grammars for reliable downstream use.
🎥 Watch: Search 'structured output LLM json schema' (outlines/instructor).
💻 Code: Force reliable JSON output from an LLM with a schema and validate it.

units.title: Knowledge graphs + LLMs
units.text:
Combining structured knowledge (graphs) with LLMs (GraphRAG) for grounded, multi-hop reasoning.
🎥 Watch: Search 'GraphRAG explained'.
💻 Code: Build a tiny knowledge graph and use it to ground/augment LLM answers (GraphRAG-lite).

units.title: Frontier reading
units.text:
Staying current: reading papers (arXiv, Papers with Code), model releases, and separating signal from hype.
🎥 Watch: Search 'how to read ML papers'.
💻 Code: Read one recent influential paper and write a one-page summary + how you'd use it.

units.title: Multimodal or generative app
units.text: [Block A] Build something with a multimodal or generative model: image search (CLIP), a captioner, or a controlled image generator. [Block B] Add structured output and evaluation where relevant; make it a real, usable tool. [Block C] Ship it with a demo + writeup — a portfolio piece that shows range beyond text LLMs.

units.title: The expanding frontier
units.text: Multimodal, diffusion, structured generation, KG+LLM and paper-reading keep you current as the field moves. Re-read your paper summary.
units.mastery: How does CLIP put images and text in one space, and how does diffusion turn noise into an image?

units.title: AI product design & UX
units.text:
Designing AI products around model strengths/weaknesses: managing uncertainty, latency, and setting user expectations.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — AI Engineering; search 'designing AI product UX'.
💻 Code: Redesign an existing feature as an AI feature, explicitly handling errors/uncertainty in the UX.

units.title: Evaluation-driven development
units.text:
Building AI features test-first: define evals, iterate against them, and treat evals as the spec.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — evaluation; search 'eval driven development LLM'.
💻 Code: For a feature, write the eval set first, then build until it passes — eval-driven.

units.title: Data flywheels
units.text:
Using production data (feedback, corrections) to continuously improve the system — the moat of AI products.
🎥 Watch: Search 'data flywheel AI product'.
💻 Code: Add a feedback-capture loop to an app that logs corrections for future improvement.

units.title: Hybrid systems (classical + LLM)
units.text:
Combining deterministic code/classical ML with LLMs — using each where it's strong (cheap/reliable vs flexible).
🎥 Watch: Search 'hybrid AI systems classical ML LLM'.
💻 Code: Build a hybrid: a cheap classifier/rules router that only calls the LLM when needed.

units.title: Case studies
units.text:
Studying real AI products (how they use retrieval, evals, guardrails, feedback) to build product judgment.
🎥 Watch: Read engineering blogs (Anthropic and others) on shipped AI features.
💻 Code: Reverse-engineer a shipped AI product into an architecture + tradeoffs writeup.

units.title: Ship a polished AI product feature
units.text: [Block A] Build a genuinely useful, polished AI feature end to end (not a demo): clear UX, error handling, evals. [Block B] Make it a hybrid where sensible (classical + LLM) and add a feedback/data-flywheel loop. [Block C] Deploy it with observability + guardrails and write the product case study — portfolio-grade AI engineering.

units.title: Building AI products
units.text: Product design, eval-driven development, data flywheels, hybrid systems and case studies are what AI engineering actually is. Re-read your case study.
units.mastery: Why is eval-driven development the right way to build with LLMs, and where should classical code do the work instead of the model?

units.title: Architecture & data
units.text:
Scope an ambitious AI system; design the architecture (retrieval/agent/model) and assemble the data/knowledge.
🎥 Watch: Reuse Chip Huyen + Anthropic agent patterns.
💻 Code: Write the AI-system design doc + architecture diagram and prepare the data/corpus.

units.title: Retrieval / agent layer
units.text:
Build the core intelligence: RAG and/or an agent with tools over your data.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your RAG + agent work.
💻 Code: Build the retrieval/agent layer with the right tools + memory.

units.title: Model integration

Build the eval harness (task success, faithfulness) and guardrails before you trust it.

units.title: Shell navigation, files, redirection & pipes
units.text:
The shell as your primary interface: navigating (cd/ls/pwd), managing files, and composing tools with pipes and redirection — the Unix philosophy.
🎥 Watch: MIT Missing Semester — the shell; 'The Linux Command Line' (Shotts) ch.1-6.
💻 Code: Do file-management + pipe tasks entirely from the shell; chain 3+ tools with pipes to answer a question.

units.title: The filesystem hierarchy (FHS)
units.text:
Where things live: /etc, /var, /usr, /home, /proc, /dev — the map of a Linux system.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux filesystem hierarchy explained'; The Linux Command Line ch.3.
💻 Code: Explore each top-level directory and note what it holds; find where a package installed its files.

units.title: Permissions & ownership (chmod, chown)
units.text:
User/group/other, read/write/execute, octal vs symbolic, and the setuid/sticky bits — Linux's security foundation.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux file permissions explained'; Missing Semester.
💻 Code: Set up a shared directory with correct group permissions and fix a 'permission denied' from first principles.

units.title: Users, groups & sudo
units.text:
Multi-user Linux: /etc/passwd + /etc/group, adding users, group membership, and sudo/root privilege.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux users and groups tutorial'.
💻 Code: Create a user + group, grant limited sudo, and verify what they can and can't do.

units.title: Package management & man pages
units.text:
Installing/updating software (apt/dnf), repositories, and reading man/--help to learn any command.
🎥 Watch: Search 'apt package management' and 'how to read man pages'.
💻 Code: Install, query and remove packages; use man + apropos to learn 3 new commands.

units.title: Scripted, reproducible Linux dev setup (dotfiles)
units.text: [Block A] Set up a Linux environment (a VM or your machine) with the tools you use; document each step. [Block B] Capture it as versioned dotfiles + an install script so it's reproducible on a fresh box. [Block C] Push a dotfiles repo with a README — a genuinely useful, on-brand portfolio repo you'll reuse.

units.title: Living on the command line
units.text: Navigation/pipes, the FHS, permissions, users/groups and package management are the daily fluency the rest of the phase assumes. Redo a task GUI-free.
units.mastery: Explain a permission string like -rwxr-xr-- fully, and what pipes + redirection let you compose.

units.title: Text tools: grep, sed, awk, cut, sort
units.text:
The text-processing power tools — grep, sed, awk, cut/sort/uniq — that make the shell a serious data tool.
🎥 Watch: Search 'awk sed grep tutorial'; Missing Semester — data wrangling.
💻 Code: Parse a log file end to end with grep/sed/awk to extract and summarize a metric.

units.title: Processes & job control
units.text:
Viewing processes (ps, top, htop), foreground/background (&, jobs, fg, bg), and signals (kill, nohup).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux process management ps top'; Julia Evans — processes.
💻 Code: Start/background/foreground jobs, find a runaway process, and kill it with the right signal.

units.title: Environment & shell configuration
units.text:
Environment variables, PATH, and shell config (.bashrc/.zshrc, aliases, functions) that shape your session.
🎥 Watch: Search 'bash environment variables PATH'; Missing Semester.
💻 Code: Customize your shell: PATH, aliases, a couple of functions, and a decent prompt.

units.title: Redirection, tee, xargs, find
units.text:
Advanced composition: stdin/stdout/stderr, tee, xargs for building commands, and find for locating/acting on files.
🎥 Watch: Search 'xargs find tutorial'; Julia Evans.
💻 Code: Use find + xargs to batch-process a directory of files and capture output with tee.

units.title: Archives, compression & file transfer
units.text:
tar/gzip/zip, rsync for efficient sync/transfer, and scp/sftp over SSH.
🎥 Watch: Search 'tar rsync tutorial'.
💻 Code: Archive + compress a directory and rsync it to another host (or VM) efficiently.

units.title: A practical shell automation toolkit
units.text: [Block A] Write shell scripts that automate real chores (backups, log parsing, batch renames, a system report). [Block B] Make them robust and composable (options, help, error handling) and put them on your PATH. [Block C] Package as a small 'toolbox' repo with a README — practical portfolio content you'll actually use.

units.title: Getting real work done in the shell
units.text: Text tools, process/job control, environment config, find/xargs and archiving are the shell as a serious work environment. Redo a chore as a one-liner.
units.mastery: How would you find and kill a runaway process, and parse a 1GB log to a summary without opening an editor?

units.title: Bash: variables, conditionals, loops
units.text:
Bash fundamentals: variables, quoting (the classic footgun), conditionals ([[ ]]) and loops.
🎥 Watch: Search 'bash scripting tutorial'; The Linux Command Line (Shotts) scripting chapters.
💻 Code: Write a script with arguments, conditionals and a loop that does something useful.

units.title: Functions, arguments & exit codes
units.text:
Functions, positional/named arguments, exit codes and $?, and returning data from functions.
🎥 Watch: Search 'bash functions exit codes'.
💻 Code: Refactor your script into functions with proper exit codes and a usage/help message.

units.title: Robust scripts: set -euo pipefail, traps
units.text:
Writing safe scripts: set -euo pipefail, error traps, cleanup on exit, and shellcheck for linting.
🎥 Watch: Search 'bash set -euo pipefail' and 'shellcheck'.
💻 Code: Harden a script with set -euo pipefail + a cleanup trap and fix every shellcheck warning.

units.title: cron & systemd timers
units.text:
Scheduling jobs with cron (crontab syntax) and the more powerful systemd timers.
🎥 Watch: Search 'crontab tutorial' and 'systemd timers vs cron'.
💻 Code: Schedule your system-report script with both a cron job and a systemd timer.

units.title: jq & structured data in the shell
units.text:
Processing JSON/YAML in the shell with jq/yq — essential for APIs and config in modern ops.
🎥 Watch: Search 'jq tutorial'.
💻 Code: Call an API with curl and use jq to extract + reshape the JSON into a report.

units.title: Automate a real workflow with a robust script
units.text: [Block A] Pick a real recurring workflow (deploy check, backup + verify, a report job) and script it end to end. [Block B] Make it production-grade: strict mode, logging, error handling/traps, config, and shellcheck-clean. [Block C] Schedule it (systemd timer) with alerting on failure and document it — a portfolio automation piece.

units.title: Scripting discipline
units.text: Bash fundamentals, functions/exit codes, robust-mode + traps, scheduling and jq turn the shell into reliable automation. Re-read your script with shellcheck.
units.mastery: Why does set -euo pipefail matter, and when do you reach for a systemd timer over cron?

units.title: systemd: units, services, journald
units.text:
systemd runs modern Linux: unit files, services, targets, enabling/starting, and reading logs with journalctl.
🎥 Watch: Search 'systemd tutorial' and 'journalctl explained'.
💻 Code: Write a systemd service unit for your automation script; enable it and read its logs via journalctl.

units.title: Networking basics: ip, ss, DNS, curl
units.text:
Inspecting/configuring the network from the shell: ip, ss (sockets), DNS (dig), and curl for HTTP debugging.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — networking zines; search 'ip ss dig tutorial'.
💻 Code: Diagnose a connectivity problem with ip/ss/dig/curl and find what's listening on a port.

units.title: SSH, keys, tmux & remote work
units.text:
SSH (key-based auth, config, tunnels), tmux for persistent sessions, and safe remote workflows.
🎥 Watch: Search 'SSH keys tutorial' and 'tmux crash course'.
💻 Code: Set up key-based SSH to a server/VM, an SSH config alias, and a tmux workflow that survives disconnects.

units.title: Disks, mounts, df/du & LVM basics
units.text:
Storage admin: partitions, filesystems, mounting, df/du for space, and LVM for flexible volumes.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux disk management df du mount' and 'LVM basics'.
💻 Code: Add/mount a disk (on a VM), find what's eating space with du, and resize a logical volume.

units.title: Log management & monitoring basics
units.text:
System logs, log rotation (logrotate), and basic health monitoring (uptime, load, memory, disk).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux logging logrotate' and system-monitoring basics.
💻 Code: Set up logrotate for your service's logs and a simple health-check script with alerting.

units.title: Provision & harden a real Linux server
units.text: [Block A] Spin up a cloud VM (or a local VM) and provision it: users, SSH keys, firewall, your service via systemd. units.title: Operating a Linux box
units.text: systemd, networking tools, SSH/tmux, storage and logging/monitoring are the core of running real servers. Re-check your server's hardening.
units.mastery: Walk through provisioning + hardening a fresh server, and how you'd debug 'the service won't start' with systemd + journalctl.

units.title: Process anatomy: address space, fds (/proc)
units.text:
What a process really is: the virtual address space (text/data/heap/stack), the fd table, and the PCB — all visible in /proc.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — processes; Julia Evans — /proc.
💻 Code: Explore /proc/<pid>/ for a running process: maps, fd, status — annotate every region.

units.title: Virtual memory & paging: page tables, TLB, COW
units.text:
Every process thinks it owns all memory; page tables translate virtual->physical, the TLB caches translations, and copy-on-write makes fork() cheap.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — virtual memory / paging.
💻 Code: Demonstrate copy-on-write: fork a process that allocated a large array and watch RSS stay shared until a write.

units.title: The page cache, dirty pages & writeback
units.text:
Free RAM isn't wasted: the kernel caches file pages (why the second read is instant); dirty pages + writeback.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux page cache explained'; Brendan Gregg.
💻 Code: Show the page cache: time a cold vs warm read of a big file; drop_caches and repeat.

units.title: Syscalls & the user/kernel boundary (strace)
units.text:
A syscall is a formal request across a security boundary (a mode switch); strace shows every one a process makes.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — strace zine; search 'Linux syscalls explained'.
💻 Code: strace a real program (e.g. one of your bots) and explain the syscall pattern you see.

units.title: Signals, zombies & the process lifecycle
units.text:
fork/exec/wait, signals (how processes are interrupted/terminated), and zombies/orphans.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — process API; Julia Evans — signals.
💻 Code: Write a program that handles signals gracefully, and create (then reap) a zombie to understand it.

units.title: Process & memory instrumentation toolkit
units.text: [Block A] Build a tool that, given a PID, reports its memory map (/proc/pid/maps), open fds, and live RSS/threads. [Block B] Add a strace-lite mode (ptrace or parse strace) that summarizes the syscalls a process makes. units.title: What a process really is
units.text: The address space + /proc, virtual memory/paging, the page cache, syscalls/strace and the process lifecycle are how programs actually run. Re-read one process's /proc.
units.mastery: Trace what happens from fork() to a running program, and why copy-on-write makes forking a 4GB process instant.

units.title: Filesystems, the VFS & inodes
units.text:
How files are stored: inodes vs names (hard/soft links), the VFS abstraction over ext4/xfs, and directories as data.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — file systems; Julia Evans — inodes.
💻 Code: Explore inodes: create hard/soft links, delete the original, and explain what survives and why.

units.title: File I/O: buffered vs direct, fsync, mmap
units.text:
How reads/writes actually hit disk: buffering, fsync for durability, O_DIRECT, and mmap for memory-mapped files.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux file IO buffered direct fsync'; OSTEP.
💻 Code: Compare throughput of buffered vs fsync-per-write vs mmap for writing a large file.

units.title: The CPU scheduler (CFS), context switches
units.text:
How Linux shares CPUs: the Completely Fair Scheduler, nice/priorities, and the cost of context switches.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — scheduling; Brendan Gregg — scheduler.
💻 Code: Observe scheduling: run CPU-bound tasks, change nice values, and measure context switches with vmstat/pidstat.

units.title: epoll & non-blocking I/O
units.text:
How servers handle thousands of connections: blocking vs non-blocking I/O and epoll (the engine under async runtimes).
🎥 Watch: Search 'epoll explained' and 'C10k problem'.
💻 Code: Write a tiny epoll-based echo server that handles many concurrent connections in one thread.

units.title: Capabilities & security primitives
units.text:
Fine-grained privileges (capabilities) beyond root, plus seccomp and namespaces as security building blocks (a bridge to containers).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux capabilities explained' and 'seccomp'.
💻 Code: Drop capabilities from a process and grant just one (e.g. bind a low port) instead of full root.

units.text: [Block A] Build a small Unix shell (C/Python): fork/exec, pipes, redirection and job control — using the syscalls directly. units.title: The network stack & sockets (ss, ip)

The layered stack (L2-L7), how a socket connects an app to the network, and inspecting it with ss/ip.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — networking zines; search 'Linux network stack explained'.
💻 Code: Map a live connection through the stack; use ss to see every socket and its state.

units.title: TCP deep: handshake, congestion control
units.text:
The 3-way handshake, flow + congestion control, TIME_WAIT, and why TCP behaves the way it does.
🎥 Watch: Search 'TCP handshake congestion control explained'; Julia Evans.
💻 Code: Watch a TCP handshake + teardown in tcpdump/Wireshark and identify each packet.

units.title: DNS, TLS, HTTP/1.1 -> HTTP/3
units.text:
How a URL becomes a response: DNS resolution, the TLS handshake, and HTTP/1.1 -> 2 -> 3 (QUIC).
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — DNS/TLS zines; search 'HTTP/2 HTTP/3 explained'.

units.title: tcpdump / Wireshark
units.text:
Packet capture and analysis — the ultimate 'what's actually on the wire' debugging tool.
🎥 Watch: Search 'tcpdump tutorial' and 'Wireshark crash course'.
💻 Code: Capture and dissect a real app's traffic; find a specific request/response in the capture.

units.title: Network tuning & throughput
units.text:
Bandwidth vs latency, buffer sizes, and diagnosing slow networks — it matters for distributed data/ML systems.
🎥 Watch: Brendan Gregg — network performance; search 'Linux network tuning'.
💻 Code: Measure throughput/latency (iperf, ping) between hosts and tune a buffer or MTU setting.

[Block C] Analyze its traffic in Wireshark and write up the request journey + your L4 LB design — a flagship networking project.

units.title: Namespaces — the isolation primitives

The Linux namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) that give a container its own view of the system — half of what a container is.

units.title: cgroups — resource limits & accounting

Control groups that limit and account CPU/memory/IO — the other half of a container; cgroups v2.

How Docker images work: layered union filesystems (overlayfs), the build cache, and image vs container.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Docker images layers overlayfs explained'; TechWorld with Nana — Docker.

How containers get networking (bridge, veth, port mapping) and persistent storage (volumes, bind mounts).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Docker networking explained' and 'Docker volumes'.

Building minimal, secure images: distroless/scratch, non-root users, vulnerability scanning and signing.

units.text:
How pods get placed (requests/limits, affinity, taints), and autoscaling (HPA) based on load.

Extending K8s with CRDs and operators that encode operational knowledge (the pattern behind data/ML platforms on K8s).

units.text:
GitOps: git as the single source of truth, with ArgoCD/Flux continuously reconciling the cluster to match.

Finding + fixing bottlenecks across CPU/memory/disk/network using the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors).
🎥 Watch: Brendan Gregg — the USE method; 'Linux performance tools'.
💻 Code: Apply the USE method to a loaded system, identify the bottleneck resource, and tune it.

units.title: Linux security: SELinux, seccomp
units.text:
Mandatory access control (SELinux/AppArmor), seccomp to restrict syscalls, and defense-in-depth for services/containers.
🎥 Watch: Search 'SELinux explained' and 'seccomp containers'.
💻 Code: Apply a seccomp profile to a container to block dangerous syscalls and observe SELinux/AppArmor denials.

units.title: Hardening & secrets
units.text:
Server/container hardening (least privilege, minimal surface, updates) and secrets hygiene end to end.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux server hardening checklist'; CIS benchmarks.
💻 Code: Run a hardening checklist against your server + containers and fix the top findings.

units.title: Cost & resource accounting
units.text:
Measuring where compute/cost goes (cgroups accounting, cloud cost), right-sizing, and FinOps for infra.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux resource accounting cgroups' and cloud cost basics.
💻 Code: Attribute resource usage per service (cgroups/cloud tags) and right-size one over-provisioned component.

units.title: Profile, tune & harden the platform
units.text: [Block A] Profile your platform under load (perf/eBPF, USE method) and fix the top performance bottleneck. [Block B] Harden it: seccomp/AppArmor on containers, a server hardening checklist, least-privilege everywhere. [Block C] Add cost/resource accounting and right-size; document the perf + security + cost wins — a rounded SRE piece.

units.title: Fast and defensible
units.text: perf/eBPF, the USE method, SELinux/seccomp, hardening and cost accounting make systems fast, secure and affordable. Re-read your flame graph.
units.mastery: Walk the USE method to find a bottleneck, and name three ways you'd harden a container running untrusted code.

units.title: Integrate the DE, ML & AI layers
units.text:
Bring the three capstones together into one intelligent platform: data flows into features, models serve predictions, an AI layer (RAG/agent) sits on top.
🎥 Watch: Review your three capstone architectures and sketch the unified one.
💻 Code: Design + wire the integration: the DE platform feeds the ML models feed the AI layer, end to end.

units.title: Deploy on Kubernetes with IaC
units.text:
Deploy the whole platform reproducibly: Terraform for infra, Helm/GitOps for the services.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your K8s + IaC + GitOps work.
💻 Code: Deploy every component to K8s via IaC + GitOps; one command from zero to running.

units.title: CI/CD & GitOps
units.text:
Automated build/test/deploy for the whole platform, with GitOps reconciliation and safe rollouts.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your CI/CD + GitOps work.
💻 Code: Wire CI/CD (test + build + deploy) and GitOps auto-sync for the platform.

units.title: Observability, alerting & SLOs
units.text:
Full-stack observability + SLOs for the integrated platform, so you'd know the moment anything degrades.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your observability/SRE work.
💻 Code: Add metrics/logs/traces, dashboards, SLOs and alerting across the whole platform.

units.title: Load & failure testing, security
units.text:
Prove it holds up: load testing, chaos/failure injection, and a security pass before you call it production.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your performance + security work.
💻 Code: Load-test the platform, inject failures (kill pods/deps) to verify resilience, and run a security pass.

units.title: Ship the intelligent platform to production
units.text: [Block A] Deploy the fully integrated DE + ML + AI platform on K8s via IaC + GitOps, with CI/CD. [Block B] Add full observability + SLOs, then load-test, chaos-test and security-harden it. [Block C] This is your capstone: the whole 62-week journey, running in production. Record a demo + architecture walkthrough.
units.demo: Intelligent data platform (DE + ML + AI) shipped to production on Kubernetes.

units.title: Everything, together, in production
units.text: Integration, K8s + IaC deploy, CI/CD + GitOps, observability + SLOs and resilience/security are the difference between projects and a platform. Step back and see the whole thing.
units.mastery: Give the full architecture tour of your platform — data to features to models to AI to serving — and how it's deployed, observed and kept reliable.

units.title: System-design writeup
units.text:
Write the definitive system-design doc for your platform: the problem, architecture, tradeoffs and lessons.
🎥 Watch: Study strong engineering system-design writeups for structure.
💻 Code: Write the full system-design doc (architecture, decisions, tradeoffs, what you'd do next).

units.title: Architecture diagrams
units.text:
Communicate the system visually: clear architecture + data-flow diagrams a stranger can follow.
🎥 Watch: Search 'good architecture diagrams C4 model'.
💻 Code: Produce clean architecture + data-flow diagrams for the platform and every capstone.

units.title: Demo & video walkthrough
units.text:
Show, don't tell: a crisp demo + recorded walkthrough that proves the work is real.
🎥 Watch: Study good project demo videos for pacing.
💻 Code: Record a tight demo/walkthrough of the platform and 2-3 flagship projects.

units.title: Blog posts / talks
units.text:
Teach what you built: writeups/talks on the standout projects (GPT from scratch, RAG, the platform) that build your reputation.
🎥 Watch: Study strong engineering blog posts for structure.
💻 Code: Write one deep technical blog post on a flagship project ('I built a GPT/container/platform from scratch').

units.title: Interview & narrative prep
units.text:
Turn 62 weeks into a story: the portfolio site, the resume update, and the interview narrative across DE/ML/AI/systems.
🎥 Watch: Review your projects and prep the STAR stories.
💻 Code: Update your portfolio + resume and rehearse the 3-minute story for each flagship project.

units.title: Portfolio launch — case studies & demos
units.text: [Block A] Assemble everything: the portfolio site, project case studies, diagrams, demos and blog posts. [Block B] Polish the top 6-8 flagship projects into strong case studies (problem -> approach -> result). [Block C] Launch it publicly (this dashboard, GitHub, LinkedIn) — the capstone of the whole journey and your new professional story.

units.title: Mastery review & what's next
units.text: Writeups, diagrams, demos, blog posts and your narrative turn 62 weeks of work into a career step. Look back at Week 1, then decide what you go deep on next.
units.mastery: Deliver your story: who you are now across Data Engineering, ML, AI and systems, and the three projects that prove it.
